notes.meaning: Elisha warned the woman whose son he had brought back to life to leave the country because a seven-year famine was coming. God sent this severe shortage of food to discipline the nation for turning away from Him. The prophet looked after this godly woman so that she and her family would be kept safe.

The woman trusted the prophet's words and moved her household to the land of the Philistines. That coastal country did not suffer from the same drought as the hills of Israel. Her quick obedience showed her faith, and God protected her family during all seven years.

When the seven years ended, the woman came back to Israel and found that others had taken over her property while she was gone. She went straight to the king's court to ask for her house and fields back. Widows and travelers often lost their property in those days, so she needed the king's ruling to regain it.

The king was talking with Gehazi, who had served Elisha, asking him to describe all the great miracles God had done through the prophet. Even though the king was not truly devoted to God, he was curious to hear these amazing true stories. This conversation set the stage for God's help to arrive at just the right moment.

While Gehazi was telling how Elisha brought a dead boy back to life, the woman and her son walked into the court to make their appeal. Gehazi immediately pointed them out to the king as living proof of the miracle. God guided the timing so that her request would be heard with special sympathy.

The king questioned the woman, and she confirmed that the story was completely true. Moved by her testimony, the king appointed an official to give back her property and all the money earned from her crops while she was gone. God repaid her faith and obedience by restoring far more than she had asked for.

Elisha traveled to the city of Damascus in Syria while King Ben-hadad was sick in bed. Word quickly reached the palace that the prophet had arrived. Even though the Syrian rulers had once tried to capture Elisha, they now respected him as a true servant of God.

King Ben-hadad told his chief servant Hazael to bring a generous gift and ask Elisha if he would recover from his illness. Sickness often makes proud rulers realize their need for God and His prophets. Ben-hadad had worshiped idols in good health, but now he turned to the God of Israel for help.

Hazael went to meet Elisha with forty camel loads of Damascus's finest treasures as a lavish gift. He greeted the prophet with deep respect and asked the king's question about whether he would survive. Calling the king Elisha's son was an ancient way of honoring the prophet as a spiritual father.

Elisha told Hazael that the king's sickness was not fatal and that he could certainly recover from it. Yet God also revealed to Elisha that Ben-hadad would still die by other means. Elisha spoke the truth about the illness itself while foreseeing the murder that Hazael would commit.

Elisha stared steadily into Hazael's face until the royal official felt uneasy and looked away. Then the prophet broke down in tears. Elisha wept because he foresaw the terrible suffering and brutality that this ambitious man would soon bring upon Israel.

Hazael asked why the prophet was crying, and Elisha described the horrific violence Hazael would commit against God's people. He would burn down Israelite forts, slaughter young men, and murder women and children in war. Elisha carried a heavy heart because he loved his people and knew the agony that awaited them.

Hazael protested that he was a nobody, using the humble term a dog, who could never have the power to do such great things. Elisha answered by revealing that God had shown him that Hazael would become the next king of Syria. Once he gained the throne, his hidden cruelty would have the power to show itself.

Hazael left Elisha and returned to his royal master, reporting only part of what the prophet had said. He claimed that Elisha promised the king would surely recover. By hiding the prophecy of death, Hazael put Ben-hadad off his guard so he could carry out his secret plot.

The next day, Hazael soaked a heavy blanket in water and spread it over the king's face until he suffocated. Because this left no marks of violence, it made the assassination look like a natural death. Hazael then seized the Syrian throne, fulfilling what God had revealed to Elisha.

Jehoram, the son of godly King Jehoshaphat, began ruling Judah while Joram was king of northern Israel. He reigned together with his father for several years before taking full power alone. This transition marked the beginning of a dark spiritual period for the southern kingdom.

Jehoram was thirty-two years old when his reign began, and he ruled in Jerusalem for eight years. His total time included years shared with his father as well as years ruling on his own. His short reign brought serious trouble and moral decay to the land of Judah.

Jehoram followed the wicked ways of the kings of northern Israel instead of his father's good example. He had married Athaliah, the daughter of wicked King Ahab, and she led him into the worship of false gods. This ungodly marriage brought deep spiritual damage and misery to Judah's royal family.

Even though Jehoram did great evil, God chose not to wipe out the kingdom of Judah. The Lord remembered His ancient covenant promise to King David to always keep a lamp, or a royal line of descendants, on his throne. This promise was kept by God's grace and ultimately pointed forward to Jesus Christ.

During Jehoram's reign, the nation of Edom rebelled against Judah's authority and set up its own king. Edom had been subject to Judah ever since the days of King David. This loss was God's discipline against Jehoram for turning his back on the Lord.

Jehoram took all his war chariots and marched out to crush the Edomite rebellion at Zair. His army was surrounded during the night, but Jehoram fought his way out and escaped, while his soldiers scattered and fled home. In the end, his military campaign failed to bring Edom back under control.

Edom remained free from Judah's control from that time on, and the city of Libnah rebelled as well. Libnah was a priestly town within Judah that apparently refused to follow Jehoram's idolatry. Because the king abandoned the true God, his kingdom quickly lost strength and broke apart.

The rest of the events of Jehoram's life and rule were recorded in the official historical annals of Judah's kings. These state records kept track of the kings' public deeds and political affairs. Other biblical passages explain that he died from a terrible and painful disease as part of God's judgment.

Jehoram died and was buried in Jerusalem, the City of David. However, the people did not bury him in the honored tombs of the kings because he was so unloved and wicked. His young son Ahaziah then succeeded him on the throne.

Ahaziah took the throne of Judah during the twelfth year of King Joram's reign over northern Israel. Both kingdoms were now ruled by young kings from families closely tied to each other by marriage. Ahaziah's reign began during a turbulent time of rising threats from neighboring nations.

Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he became king, and his reign in Jerusalem lasted only one year. His mother was Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab and granddaughter of King Omri of Israel. She raised him under the corrupt influence of her idolatrous family.

Ahaziah walked in the evil ways of Ahab's dynasty, practicing idolatry and disobeying God. Because his mother and her relatives guided his royal court, he adopted the corrupt customs of northern Israel. Being so closely linked to an ungodly household brought ruin upon him and his nation.

Ahaziah formed an alliance with his uncle, King Joram of Israel, to fight against King Hazael of Syria at Ramoth-gilead. Just as Ahab and Jehoshaphat had fought together at the same fortress years before, their descendants now joined forces in battle. During the fighting, the Syrian archers wounded King Joram.

King Joram left the battlefield and retreated to his palace at Jezreel to heal from his battle wounds. Ahaziah traveled down to Jezreel to visit his injured uncle and show family support. By God's sovereign plan, this visit placed Ahaziah in the very city where judgment was about to fall upon the house of Ahab.
